pages.hook: In the USA, people with many different diets eat at the same market. Asking “What’s in this?” is normal, polite and sometimes very important for health.
pages.polite: Say **I don’t eat pork** or **I’m allergic to peanuts**. Then ask, **Do you have something else?**

mythfact.s: It is normal to ask what is in a dish.
mythfact.why: Cooks and servers expect the question.

mythfact.s: In the USA, food labels show nothing about allergies.
mythfact.why: US labels must name major allergens like milk, eggs, peanuts and wheat.

mythfact.s: San Francisco has a famous Chinatown with many dumpling shops.
mythfact.why: It is one of the oldest Chinatowns in North America.

mythfact.s: “Vegan” food has no meat, no fish, no eggs and no milk.
mythfact.why: Vegan = no animal products.

mythfact.s: Being allergic is the same as not liking a food.
mythfact.why: An allergy can make you sick; saying “I don’t like it” is different.

decode.why: The vegan veggie dumplings have no meat.

compare.br: In Brazil, “feijão com arroz” is an everyday meal, and people often ask the cook, “Tem carne?” before they eat.
compare.us: In the USA, many people say clearly what they can’t eat: I’m vegan, I’m allergic to nuts, I don’t eat pork.
compare.tip: Use “I don’t eat…” for a rule and “I’m allergic to…” for health.
compare.ask: Is there a food you don’t eat? Say it in English.

quiz.q: You want to know the filling. You ask…
quiz.why: What’s in it? asks about the ingredients.

quiz.q: You don’t eat pork. You say…

quiz.why: Six for eight dollars = six dumplings for $8.

pages.title: Cultural spotlight · Quiz
Reading quest — The dumpling stand · part 1
text: Mei has a small dumpling stand in **San Francisco**. Every day, people come and say, “**Yum!** These smell good.” Mei smiles. “**Try one**,” she says.

One day, a woman called Nina comes to the stand. “**What’s in it?**” she asks. “Pork and cabbage,” says Mei. “**I don’t eat pork**,” says Nina. “**Do you have** chicken?” “Yes! Chicken and mushroom,” says Mei.
Nina eats one. “**Perfect!** How much?” “**Six for eight dollars**,” says Mei. Nina buys six, and she tries the sauce. It is a little spicy. “**It’s fire!**” she laughs, and drinks some water.

opts: A woman buys dumplings at a stand

scan.q: What does Nina not eat?
How many dumplings cost eight dollars?
Who collected the fairy tale in 1812?

tf.s: Mei sells dumplings in San Francisco.
tf.why: “A small dumpling stand in San Francisco.”

tf.s: Nina eats pork.
The sauce is a little spicy.
The fairy tale is from Italy.

order: Mei says, “Try one.”
Nina asks what is in the dumplings.
Nina chooses chicken and mushroom.
Nina pays eight dollars for six.
Nina comes back the next week.

pages.title: Reading quest — The dumpling stand · part 2
text: Mei thinks about her grandmother’s story. It is a fairy tale from Germany, “Hansel and Gretel”. The Brothers Grimm collected it in 1812. Two children find a house of bread, cake and candy. “Are these sweet?” they ask. Mei’s dumplings are not sweet, but the children in her street love them too.
Nina comes back the next week. “**Enjoy the dumplings!**” says Mei. Now Nina is a happy customer, and she tells her friends about the little stand.
